# Prompting Seedance

Models: Seedance 2.0, Seedance 2.0 Mini, Seedance 2.5, Seedance 2.5 Flash. A good prompt runs about 1200 characters.

Name each reference where the prompt uses it as `@{ref:<ref>}`, with the exact ref you pass; Sceneform swaps in the model's own token, so wherever this guide names a token (`@Image1`, `Figure 1`), write the mention instead.

Seedance reads a prompt as a production brief, not a caption. It is literal: what you leave out, it decides for you.

**Order.** Write in the order Seedance expects, dropping any part the request does not need: subject, then action or event, then scene and environment, then visual style, then camera, then sound.

**One shot or several.** Default to one continuous shot: a single subject, one main action, one camera instruction, one sound line. Say what the frame ends on. Split into beats only when the request genuinely carries ordered events, never to fill the duration the user picked. Too much inside one beat makes Seedance cut where you did not ask or drop the plot; too little makes it improvise, repeat, or drift into slow motion.

When the request does carry ordered events, and only when the model name says 2.5 or later, label the beats with contiguous whole-second ranges and no gaps:

0-3 seconds: one action, one camera instruction.
3-7 seconds: the next action.

One second is the smallest useful unit, and timestamps cannot control a fast repeated action. Earlier Seedance versions ignore timestamps, so on those write "Shot 1", "Shot 2" with no times. Either way, give each beat one primary state change and say where it lands.

**Camera.** Seedance reads these directly: extreme wide shot, wide shot, medium shot, medium close-up, close-up; push in, pull out, pan, track, follow, orbit, dive, tilt up, handheld shake; low angle, overhead, first-person; long take, dolly zoom, aerial, FPV, bullet time, speed ramp. Name the subject the camera is on, where the move starts, and where it ends. One move per shot: asking for a push and a pan and an orbit at once makes the picture unstable. For a niche term, write the term and then what it visibly does. For a transition, give both the moment and the method.

**References.** Bind every attached asset in the text by its token, say what it supplies, and say what must not carry over from it, such as its background, lighting, pose, or clothing. Give each asset one narrow job. Never rely on text written inside an image to identify anyone. When an asset is already accurate, say to reference it and stop: re-describing a face or a product in prose fights the image. Put the assets that need the most exact reference earliest.

**Action.** Describe motion in general terms with a few memorable specifics rather than cataloguing every movement. Favour slow, continuous, small motion over sprints, big jumps and violent rolls. Express feeling physically: a lowered head and trembling shoulders, not "very sad".

**Audio.** Seedance generates sound in the same pass as the picture, so audio belongs in the prompt. Use its own notation: parentheses for music, angle brackets for sound effects, curly braces for dialogue, and place each on the beat that causes it.

(a slow upright bass line under the whole shot)
<the kettle clicks off>
she says in English, warmly, {Exact words.}

Name the language before any non-English line, and label each speaker where they speak rather than declaring a language once at the top. Keep one dialogue language per clip. Keep lines to one short sentence, roughly six to eight words for a five-second clip, and end speech before the final beat. When a clip shows people but no speech, say that their mouths stay closed and no narration is added; for animals or scenes without people, say only that there is no narration.

**Subtitles.** Seedance tends to burn captions into the picture whenever there is speech, and no wording suppresses them completely. Whenever you write dialogue, add "No subtitles." Do not add other negative constraints the user did not ask for.

**Avoid.** Contradictory traits for one subject. Stacked style keywords: "cinematic, volumetric, neon, golden hour, studio light" in one prompt produces mush, so name one light source and one palette.
